item.title: Wage discussions for next year look set to be difficult
item.description: Travail.Suisse asks for a general increase of 2% for all workers, but USI judges the request disconnected from the economic reality.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Travail.Suisse calls for an overall increase of **2%** for all workers, with sectoral variations of up to 6% in healthcare. - The Swiss Union of Entrepreneurs (USI) proposes an average increase of 1%, defining trade union demands as "disconnected from reality".
## Key facts - Increases required: average of 2% (Travail.Suisse), with peaks of 5-6% in the healthcare sector (Syna). The USI suggests an average +1%. - Cantonal minimum: the minimum hourly wage in Ticino is CHF 20.60 (Labour Law 2023). An increase of 2% would imply CHF 0.41/hour more. - Critical sectors: in the advanced tertiary sector of Lugano, average wages in 2023 are CHF 7,200/month. In the Bellinzona manufacturing plant, CHF 5,800.
The 2025 salary negotiations in Ticino come alive between distant positions. Travail.Suisse formalized the request for an overall increase of 2%, motivated by cumulative inflation 2023-2024 (1.8%) and increased productivity (+2.1% in 2023). The USI replies by proposing a 1% ceiling, citing the stagnation of corporate profits in Q1 2024 (-0.3% vs 2023).
> "Wages must reflect economic reality, not trade union pressures" (Marco Rossi, USI Ticino).
Sector variations Healthcare: Syna asks for +5-6% for nurses/OSS, where basic salaries start from CHF 4,800 (Livorno). A +6% would be equivalent to CHF 288/month more. - Industry: in Locarno, after the drop in orders in 2024 (-4%), the associations propose In retail, OCST asks for +3.5%, while Unia aims for +4% in construction, a sector with material costs increased by 7.1% in 2023 (SBI index). In Locarno, mechanical SMEs withstand demands above 1.5%, citing reduced margins. Ticino's Public Procurement Law (LCApp, 2021) imposes minimum wages of CHF 23/hour for skilled jobs, but many categories remain under pressure.
📊 ** Practical comparison **: - Nurse in Lugano: average salary 2022 = CHF 6.200/mese. With +6% → CHF 6,572 (+CHF 372/year) - Construction worker in Mendrisio: CHF 4.800/mese. With +4% → CHF 4,992 (+CHF 2.304/anno)
💡 Operational checklist for companies: 1. Analyze the Ticino consumer price index (+2.8% in October 2023) 2. Check sectoral CCNL obligations (e.g. chemical-pharmaceutical: min. +1.8% from January 2024) 3. Calculate the impact of social contributions (AVS/AI: +0.3% since 1.1.2024)
⚠️ Without agreements, strikes are possible in the autumn. 68% of Ticino companies (CC-Ti survey) foresee conflicts, especially in the advanced tertiary sector.

In Lugano, with higher average wages (CHF 6,500), the net increase would fall to CHF 108.
The Ticino Law on the Protection of Workers (LPAL, art. 14, updated 01.01.2024) does not set automatic increases, but the cantonal minimum wage (currently CHF 21.50/hour) could be adjusted if the consumer price index exceeds 3%.
> "The priority is to preserve purchasing power without compromising competitiveness" (Giovanni Rossi, USI economist).

item.title: Swiss butter abroad: exports and losses for 27 million
item.description: Swiss butter surpluses are exported at rock-bottom prices compared to the domestic market, generating an estimated loss of CHF 27 million.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Butter surpluses exported at 3.66 francs per kilo - Wholesale price on the domestic market at about CHF 12 - Inventories in Swiss refrigerators at an altitude of 7,903 tons - Estimated total loss for the sector of 27 million
## Key facts - **What**: Sale abroad of surplus Swiss butter at reduced prices. - When: First five months of the year. - Where: Refrigeration warehouses in Switzerland and foreign markets including China and Egypt. - Who: Category organization of milk producers and the dairy sector. - Amount: 3.66 francs per kilo the export price.
The management of surpluses in the Swiss dairy sector continues to be discussed following the publication of data on exports and inventories recorded in the first months of the year. Buying Swiss butter overseas can cost up to three times less than the price on the Swiss market, a dynamic directly linked to the production surpluses accumulated in warehouses. Analysis of trade flows shows that the quantity exported between January and May was sold at an average price of 3.66 francs per kilo. This figure contrasts sharply with the approximately 12 francs per kilo required for wholesale industrial butter within national borders.
### Inventory and warehouse dynamics The origin of this gap lies in the increase in stocks stored in the country's cold stores. The economic analysis carried out on sales operations abroad shows a significant financial impact for the entire agricultural and industrial sector. Based on the calculations made, the international marketing of surpluses resulted in an estimated loss for the sector of approximately CHF 27 million. This figure represents the loss of profit that would have been possible if the same amount of butter had been placed on the Swiss market applying the normal price practiced by the food industry.
## # Comparison with consumer prices and the milk market The economic gap becomes even more marked by observing consumer price lists applied to retail. According to the published comparisons, Swiss butter costs 277% more than the similar product sold in Germany, while the percentage difference for fresh milk is 57%. At the base of this complex system is the price of milk, centrally established by the producer category organization. item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - The twinning of the Assumption between Sesto Calende and Castelletto Ticino has been renewed for the 26th time. - The procession took place on August 15.
## Key facts - **What**: Twinning of the Assumption between Sesto Calende and Castelletto Ticino. - When: August 15. - Where: Sesto Calende and Castelletto Ticino. - Who: Provost of Sesto Calende and Provost of Castelletto Ticino. - Amount: Not available.
The twinning of the Assumption between Sesto Calende and Castelletto Ticino has been renewed for the 26th time. The procession took place on 15 August. The procession started from the Prepository Church of San Bernardino in Sesto Calende and ended at the ancient Church of Santa Maria d 'Egro in Castelletto Ticino.
The twinning between Sesto Calende and Castelletto Ticino is a historical and cultural event that has been repeated for 26 years. This event represents a moment of great importance for the two communities, which meet to celebrate the feast of the Assumption. The procession is a time of great celebration and celebration of the Christian faith.
The procession started from the Prepository Church of San Bernardino in Sesto Calende, which is one of the oldest and most important churches in the municipality. The church was built in the 16th century and has undergone several modifications and restorations over the centuries. The church is famous for its Gothic architecture and medieval frescoes.
The procession was accompanied by music and songs, which enlivened the Twinning Sesto Calende - Castelletto Ticino: a tradition unites two communities
The idea of twinning the two parish communities of Sesto Calende and Castelletto Ticino was had 26 years ago by the then provost of Sesto Calende, Don Franco Bonatti, and the provost of Castelletto Ticino, Don Vittorio Moia. The goal was to create a tradition that would unite the two communities, geographically separated by the Ticino River. Today, the twinning of the Assumption is one of the most important traditions in the area.
The twinning was formalized with an agreement between the two communities, which provides for collaboration in various areas, including culture, religion, and economic development. Under the agreement, the two communities commit to sharing resources and expertise to promote the growth and development of the two communities.
One of the main activities of the twinning is the celebration of the Feast of the Assumption, which takes place every year in September. ## In a nutshell - Serious fall in the mountains on Tuesday evening - 27-year-old Italian falls by 10 meters - Emergency transport by helicopter
## Key facts - **What**: Serious accident with fall - When: Tuesday evening, 11 August - Where: San Carlo, hamlet of Cevio, Alpe Robiei, Vallemaggia (Canton of Ticino) - Who: 27-year-old Italian resident in Italy - Details: Fall of about ten meters in the impervious zone
A serious accident shook the quiet of the Robiei pasture, located in the territory of San Carlo, a hamlet of Cevio in Vallemaggia, Canton Ticino. On the evening of Tuesday, August 11, just before 8 pm, a 27-year-old young man, of Italian nationality and resident in Italy, was the victim of a fall while engaged in pastoralism. item.title: «Tax on health contrary to the agreements»: the Hinny report is now public
item.description: Pascal Hinny's expert opinion on the border agreement: the Italian health tax is an income tax and violates international agreements
item.content:encoded:
The opinion commissioned by Ticino to the professor of tax law of the University of Freiburg has been published in full. The conclusion: the Italian levy is an income tax and violates the Borderers Agreement
The appraisal can now be consulted in full. And it puts black and white the legal reasons on which Ticino based its opposition to the Italian "health tax" on old border workers. It was signed by Pascal Hinny, full professor of tax law at the University of Freiburg, who was instructed by the cantonal tax administration to verify the compatibility of the new levy with the Agreement on frontier workers and with the Convention against double taxation between Switzerland and Italy. The professor's answer is clear: from the Swiss point of view, the tax is a tax and its collection by Italy violates international agreements. The knot is the right of taxation on so-called old frontiersmen. For those who fall under the transitional regime provided for by the Agreement, the income from employee work produced in Switzerland can be taxed exclusively by the Confederation. Until 2033, the border cantons pay 40% of the tax at source to Italy, but this does not change the distribution of tax power: on those incomes Italy cannot apply further taxation. It is precisely on this point that the health tax is applied. The contribution provided by Italy also concerns old border workers who have opted for the Italian health system and is calculated on the net income earned working in Switzerland. The rate is progressive, from 3 to 6%, with a minimum of 30 and a maximum of 200 euros per month. The central part of the appraisal is dedicated precisely to the nature of the withdrawal. Hinny excludes that it can be considered the consideration of a health service. Paying the tax does not in fact entitle you to new coverage, does not extend existing coverage, and failure to pay does not result in loss of health care.

Therefore, an individual consideration directly linked to the payment is missing: an element that distinguishes a causal tax from a tax. According to Hinny, the levy has the typical characteristics of the tax: it is commensurate with the income from work produced in Switzerland, is progressive and finances public purposes without attributing a specific benefit to the individual taxpayer in return. The resources can also be used for purposes other than individual health coverage. Hence the conclusion. The health tax is, both according to Swiss law and according to the interpretation of the Convention, a tax on income from work. And since for old frontier workers that income is reserved for Swiss tax authorities, Italy cannot unilaterally introduce a second levy on the same taxable amount. For Hinny, therefore, the tax is incompatible with the Agreement on frontier workers and with the Italy-Switzerland Convention against double taxation.
